newsitem.title: USA: Miami city manager gives assurance on bonds.
newsitem.headline: Miami city manager gives assurance on bonds.

text.p: Acting Miami City Manager Merrett Stierheim gave assurances Thursday that the city's budget shortfall would not prevent it from paying debt service on its bonds.
"We're going to be cutting services, people, salaries, raising all kinds of fees and things before we would think about not paying our bonds," Stierheim told Reuters.

Stierheim estimated the city has a $60 million deficit in its $275 million budget for fiscal 1997, which began Tuesday. He called an emergency meeting for Monday to discuss remedies but said it would be premature to predict how many workers might be laid off.
Moody's Investors Service put its single-A rating for Miami's general obligation under review with negative implications last week, citing the budget problems.
Asked if he expected Standard & Poor's to take similar action with its single-A rating, Stierheim said, "It's not going to surprise me but I would hope they wouldn't."
Fitch Investors Service does not rate any Miami bonds.

Stierheim was appointed after the resignation of City Manager Cesar Odio, who was charged by federal prosecutors in an alleged bribery scheme involving city contracts. Former City Finance Director Manohar Surana has agreed to plead guilty to unspecified related charges, prosecutors said.
Stierheim has asked city attorneys to investigate the possibility of legal action against Surana.

"Clearly there was a tremendous amount of misinformation or disinformation in the budget, which he prepared," Stierheim said. "The finance director submitted it as a balanced budget when in fact within 48 hours (of becoming city manger) I knew that wasn't a balanced budget. I just didn't know how imbalanced it was."
Stierheim said the $60 million deficit figure could still rise because he was awaiting more information on capital expenditures.

He has also asked the city's external auditors, Deloitte & Touche, to attend Monday's budget meeting. The firm's last report, delivered in September, said "there is more to be done" to improve city finances, but gave no indication of the seriousness of its budget problems.
"I'm sure the mayor and commissioners are going to ask them questions," Stierheim said. "It's hard to understand how this situation could have gone really as seriously undetected."
Deloitte & Touche officials were out of town at a meeting and were unavailable for comment.
Miami Herald also reported Thursday that state auditors discovered in 1993 that Miami had "deteriorating financial condition trends" but did not tell anyone because they were not required to.
The April 1983 report was part of a proposal from the Auditor General's Office, which tried unsuccessfully to persaude the Legislature to establish a monitoring system for local government finances.
Ted Sauerbeck, supervisor of local government audits, told the newspaper that the report was confidential under Florida public records law.
Stierheim was incredulous at the report. "Its amazing that an arm of the state government would not in some way, discreetly or otherwise, raise the flag," he said.
